quote: Nobody down the line answers him.
why: reports a collective absent reaction as evidence of the moment's weight instead of rendering an actual physical detail or a specific character's response
suggestion: Cut it, or replace with a specific reaction: "Kavi looks at the grass in front of his own feet."

rule_name: STYLE_RULES 4: Invented similes versus inherited similes
quote: a tenth of a second up there is most of a house
why: a newly built, writerly spatial comparison delivered in narration rather than in a character's mouth
suggestion: Cut the comparison and state the fact plainly: "because a tenth of a second up there is several metres of flight."

quote: They hear it before they see anything
why: routes the arrow-collision sound through the perception verb "hear" instead of rendering the stimulus directly
suggestion: "A small dry click sounds a long way up, before anything is visible."

quote: she is not sure for a second whether she made it up
why: "for a second" is the banned generic duration filler, used in a chapter that otherwise measures time precisely
suggestion: Cut the filler: "she is not sure whether she made it up."

quote: she keeps looking at the table for a while
why: "for a while" is the banned universal duration marker, doing no specific work here
suggestion: "she keeps looking at the table until Sam reaches for another roll"

quote: with her back against the side of the bath for a while
why: second instance of "for a while" as a generic duration marker rather than a real, specific one
suggestion: "with her back against the side of the bath until the tap in the next room shuts off"

rule_name: STYLE_RULES 8: Automatic-fail narrator constructions (superlatives in narration)
quote: The strongest version anybody has put on paper
why: a narrator superlative ranking the source material instead of describing what makes it strong
suggestion: "A man writing in 1961 gets closer than anyone else she reads"

rule_name: STYLE_RULES 8: Automatic-fail narrator constructions (superlatives in narration)
quote: do the most damage to what he has built
why: second narrator superlative in the same paragraph, ranking the objections instead of naming them
suggestion: "finds three objections he never answers"

quote: She notices that happening while it is happening
why: filters her own mood-shift through "notices" instead of letting the shift stand on its own
suggestion: Cut the sentence; the prior sentence already renders the change.

quote: She notices that happening while it is happening, but she does not know what to do about it.
why: explains the shift from angry to interested that the preceding sentence already showed
suggestion: Cut the sentence and end the beat on "started being interested."

quote: is not an argument, it is a request
why: defines the argument by what it is not before stating what it is, the exact "not A, but B" pattern the rule bans
suggestion: "An argument you apologise for is a request."

quote: is not an argument, it is a request
why: the not-X-but-Y construction is an automatic-fail in narration per the table; it is only sanctioned in dialogue
suggestion: State the point directly: "An argument you apologise for is a request."

quote: He's right,
why: a bare verdict construction, a close variant of the explicitly banned "you're right"
suggestion: "Page nine and twenty-two are the only two he found," Chloe says, and sits down where she is with the pages on her knees.

quote: in a tone that suggests he does not mean it
why: loads the dialogue tag with a prepositional explanation of tone instead of showing it through action or letting the line stand alone
suggestion: "'Good luck,' Sinclair says. The line goes dead before the second word finishes landing."

rule_name: STYLE_RULES 1: Point of view and tense
quote: Ruth ends up running the east stairwell, because she starts giving orders inside the first thirty seconds and everybody standing on those stairs does what she tells them.
why: reports action at a stairwell Chloe has no way to witness (she is on the third-floor landing for the whole exercise) without the signalled camera exception or an established overhearing device
suggestion: Frame it as something Chloe hears afterward: "Ruth, people say afterward, ran the east stairwell from the first thirty seconds."

quote: the first ninety seconds of the whole thing
why: "the whole thing" is the banned vague catch-all crutch phrase standing in for "the Watch," which the surrounding paragraphs already name
suggestion: "the first ninety seconds of the Watch"

quote: Chloe spends the whole of it on the third floor landing
why: "the whole of it" is a vague stand-in for "the Watch," a close variant of the banned "the whole thing"
suggestion: "Chloe spends the whole Watch on the third floor landing"

quote: She can hear the six on the floor below hitting theirs.
why: routes the sound of the floor below through "can hear" instead of rendering it directly
suggestion: "Below, six more crack theirs against the stairwell."

rule_name: STYLE_RULES 1: Point of view and tense
quote: puts his glasses back on, and asks the boy nearest him whether he is done with the Burke
why: reports Hearn's exact gesture and words in the library, a location Chloe never leaves the third-floor landing to reach, with no camera-exception signal or established source for the detail
suggestion: Move the beat to a retelling the next day rather than narrating it live, e.g. have Sam or the board report it secondhand.

quote: She stands in front of that one for a while
why: third instance of "for a while" used as a generic, non-specific duration marker
suggestion: "She stands in front of that one through the next bell."
